title: Show HN: I recreated "Crazy Ones" ad as an animated web tribute to Steve Jobs
text:
Today marks 15 years since Steve Jobs died. I remember watching his narrated version of "Here’s to the crazy ones" that day and crying. It felt like he was reading his own obituary. The ad suddenly seemed to have been about him all along.

When I first saw the original as a teenager, I decided to buy a Mac. It took me four years of saving. I still think it’s the best ad ever made: it never mentions a product, but it sold me on the whole company.

To mark the anniversary, I recreated it as an animated monochrome experience that runs in the browser, with Jobs' original narration.

I used Claude Opus 5.5 (ultracode) for the code, animation, and sound design, GPT-Image-2.5 for the illustrations, and ElevenLabs for the music. The voice is Jobs’s actual recording, isolated from the original soundtrack.

title: Re: Anthropic Subscriptions Offer 5x+ More Value Than ...
text:
This is a great first step for comparison, but I wish they paired this $ amount comparison to units of output.

Consider the data from https://artificialanalysis.ai :

| Model | intelligence score | price for full suite | total tokens for suite |

| Sonnet 5.5_| 56 | $9,074 | 416M |

| Opus 5.5__| 58 | $8,708 | 260M |

| Sol 6.1____| 52 | $1,536 | _67M |

For a fixed set of tasks, the anthropic models (do score higher) but cost much more (both because per token prices are higher and because total token counts are higher).

So it isn't at all obvious that the anthropic subscription is more value. Anthropic's models cost more per token, which explains a large amount of the "value" difference you get from the plan. Then even if you look at tokens, you'er only getting ~3x more tokens from Anthropic which is not even enough to close the Opus-Sol6.1 efficiency gap.

title: Re: Vast-10M: Technical Report...
text:
Hi HN, Here is the technical report for a family of LLMs my co-founder and I built with ten million tokens of context. It's really a proof of concept for a new kind of attention, called VSA (Voltropy Scalable Attention.)

There were previously two approaches to getting context to work at this scale. One was to approximate attention in ways that degraded reasoning-quality at lower context lengths. The other was to abandon the transformer architecture in favor of cheaper alternatives that only did e.g. recurrent computation, like state space models.

We designed VSA to be a third path: One that would extend context by an order of magnitude while also increasing reasoning quality at shorter contexts. And what is striking about the results we share today is that this worked, even when we retrofitted VSA to transformers that were training with conventional attention.

When we augmented DeepSeek v4.0 Flash with VSA, the resulting model scored better at ten million tokens than the original did at one million tokens. To our surprise, it did even better than DeepSeek's next-generation model, v4.1 Flash. In fact, the 1M-token performance was so strong that it beat Anthropic's Fable 5.1 by around 10%.

All this is to say that we believe we've found an important new primitive for building LLMs. As we discuss in the blog post, we think that this could scale way beyond 10M tokens, and that stretching it to billions or trillions of tokens could fundamentally reshape what LLMs are.

First, it could solve continual learning, by making context windows so large that agents can learn continuously within ever leaving a context window. Basically, a loophole to solve continual learning without post-deployment weight updated.

Second, it could allow for much of the data that is currently stored in weights through lossy memorization to be moved into a structured, context-like format. Basically, the goal would be to make LLMs less like human brains and more like classical Von Neumann machines.

Obviously, that vision requires scaling VSA far beyond where it is today. But we're excited to share this first step on the journey with you all.

title: Show HN: Use macOS shortcuts on Windows
text:
Hi HN!

In my day to day, I switch between my Windows PC and Macbook often. One thing I find annoying is having to change what keyboard shortcuts I use depending on the OS (e.g. cmd+c vs ctrl+c for copying). It confuses my muscle memory and slows me down.

I first tried using AutoHotkey to bind MacOS-like shortcuts to Windows shortcuts. This worked, but it was hard to configure. I would also have to quit AutoHotkey to get past Anti-Cheat software on some games.

So I decided to create this app in case others also face the same issues as me.

Disclaimer: I built this app using Claude Code. I don't have much experience building windows apps so it would've been difficult to make this on my own.

title: Show HN: Rashomon – An independent execution record for AI coding agents
text:
I have been working on Rashomon, an open-source execution recorder for AI coding agents.

The basic idea is that the agent transcript is not ground truth. Rashomon keeps its own record of what happened and compares it against the agent’s account.

For Claude Code, it records things like:

* shell commands, exit codes, and whether they may have written files * tool calls and outcomes * test commands and their outcomes * subagent lifecycle and ordering * timestamps and parent/child relationships * keyed digests of command/tool inputs and working directories

It builds a timeline from these events. It does not store prompts, responses, file contents, or tool output.

For example, it now detects patterns like:

`test fails → only test files change → same test passes`

and:

`test command fails → same command passes → no corresponding file edit`

These can indicate that an agent changed a test instead of fixing the underlying issue.

Rashomon currently runs as a Claude Code plugin or through the CLI.

CLI:

`rashomon watch`

then:

`rashomon report`

Plugin:

`/rashomon:report`

There are still edge cases around cwd, git state, test-selection arguments, generated files, retries, and parallel execution. I would be interested in feedback from people building agents on what execution signals you would want Rashomon to capture or correlate.

GitHub: https://github.com/altrace-dev-role/rashomon
author: rganupa

title: Re: Show HN: Rashomon – An independent execution recor...
text:
Rashomon is an independent execution recorder for coding agents that notifies users whenever there is a discrepancy between what the agent said it did and what we capture as a ground truth.

My team and I were working on a different project and we faced a problem with being able to verify what an agent did, rather than relying on its own transcript.

It aims to capture items like shell commands, exit codes, file writes, tool calls, tests, and subagents. We build a timeline of the events but we do not store any prompts, responses, file contents, or tool outputs.

To get started, you can install it is as a Claude Code plugin or from the command line.

I would appreciate feedback on any edge cases as well as what execution items people want captured that we do not do already.

title: Re: Interfaze-1-lite: the first open-weight model for ...
text:
Hey HN! Today we’re releasing interfaze-1-lite, an open-weight model for tasks with a deterministic answer: OCR, speech-to-text with speaker diarization, classification, structured extraction and object detection.

The problem we had been facing: when the consumer of a model’s output is not a human but another piece of code, having a 95% accurate model was not enough to automate things without knowing which 5% were correct. Chat models cannot do this, hence someone needs to verify the answers anyway.

Lite is a reasoning core plus a collection of specialist models (document reader, line detector, speech recognizer, segmentation). The core chooses the specialists to be executed and produces the answer in your JSON schema.

The specialist models give you: bounding boxes, word timestamps and a confidence score per each line and word. The raw outputs are returned next to the answer so that you can filter based on that. E.g., post rows above 0.9 automatically and forward the rest to a human.

Benchmarks against Gemini-3.7-Flash, Claude-Sonnet-5, GPT-5.4-Mini and Grok-4.3, where Lite does the best: - MMMU-Pro: 73.2% - RefCOCO: 83.8% - Structured output (SOB): 81.5% - olmOCR: 83.8% - VoxPopuli WER: 3.0%

Runs on a single 80 GB GPU (e.g. H100) without any additional services.

Blog post: https://interfaze.ai/blog/the-first-open-weight-model-for-de...

Happy to answer any questions regarding the architecture, benchmarks and limitations.

title: Ask HN: Anybody else enjoying Cursor's native (xAI) models?
text:
Regardless of whatever the latest flagship models can do, I've always thought Cursor has had the best agentic IDE experience around the models. Not necessarily giving the best results overall--since that is very dependent on the strength of the models you use, and always using the flagship models can be a real difference--but as for everything around the actual models, Cursor is up there, if not the best, in my humble opinion.

Lately, however, using Cursor's built-in models, since they give you way more usage for those, I have been really impressed. Before, if it wasn't the latest and greatest model from OpenAI or Anthropic (especially Anthropic), it always felt like I was getting less.

For me, the frontier around Opus 4.6 was when agentic coding started really feeling real. As long as you asked something that was possible, and asked in the right way (know precisely what you want, and being reasonably specific), the models could genuinely do anything a human developer could do, and do it well. (Or at least, the vast majority of the time, that is.) That was huge for me, and I pretty much exclusively relied on higher tier models from there on, as some of the projects I work on are very gnarly.

With Cursor Grok 4.6 though, for the first time, it has reached that level. It shouldn't feel this way, because it still feels like I'm paying for cheap Chinese or open-source (no offense intended) models, but I can't complain since these models just give me what I'm asking for, without any of the pain that's I'm used to. If ever I'm not getting the results I want , for the vast majority of the time, I honestly can't say it's the model's fault. Frustration with output has become remarkably rare for me, and Grok 4.7 is even a step up from that!

This, along with the fact that as long as you don't enable the fast option or higher context windows, it's almost impossible to use all your included usage, has made the value proposition for Cursor really incredible for me. I pay $20 a month, and I can (not exaggerating) do several competent 100,000 LOC+ refactors every month without even hitting 50% on included Cursor models usage. It's wild.

I bring this all up though to ask: why is nobody talking about this? I'm not paid by anyone to endorse anything. I'm just a guy. But as a guy who is thoroughly impressed, it's my opinion that this is by far the best offer in the space right now. OpenAI and Anthropic have better models, and therefore offer better results, but the performance gap is genuinely not much, and the corresponding prices are definitely not this cheap, nor the access this available. That and the fact that the surrounding IDE is pleasure to use makes me think that more people should be aware of this.

title: Show HN: Abralo - Open source Slack for agents and people
text:
Hi guys,

Posted this (https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=48832797) on HN a few months ago when it was a different product (and closed source). It was originally a way of managing multiple agents in parallel (like TMUX, but with a nicer chat UI).

But I found that I was only able to work with 3 or 4 agents simultaneously without information overload, so I decided to morph it into something which resembles Slack, where you can either privately speak to agents or address a room (like a channel) full of them. Importantly though, the agents can delegate work to each other, create other agents etc.

Also had lots of user feedback from the first launch which means we've added multiple harnesses (Codex, OpenCode and waiting for Anthropic to approve Claude Code), git worktrees, connections to hundreds of MCPs, CLIs and APIs, browser-use and a proactive Chief of Staff (which periodically wakes up and gets things moving). It's local with no telemetry.

Grateful for the feedback from our users from the first launch. Would be grateful for bug reports, other problems, ideas, questions or suggestions.

Thanks, Chris
